list.listitem: Suspect irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in patients with abdominal pain and altered bowel habits for at least 3 to 6 months. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis.C

Initial evaluation in primary care should include a complete blood count, C-reactive protein or sedimentation rate, and serology for celiac disease. For patients younger than 45 years who present with diarrhea, order a fecal calprotectin test to rule out inflammatory bowel disease.C

Colonoscopy needs to be done only when alarm features are present, the patient is not current on colorectal cancer screening, or if they are at increased risk for microscopic colitis (female, at least 50 years old, with comorbid autoimmune disease; weight loss; diarrhea for less than 12 months; or severe, nocturnal, or watery diarrhea).B
Exercise and increasing doses of soluble fiber (eg, ispaghula) but not insoluble fiber (eg, wheat bran) are recommended first-line treatments.B. B
Second-line drugs in primary care include tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.B
ACG guidelines recommend a trial of a low FODMAPS diet and gut-directed psychotherapy.B
Drug therapies recommended by ACG guidelines include rifaximin for IBS with diarrhea, and lubiprostone or linaclotide for IBS with constipation.B

background.definition: Irritable bowel syndrome is defined as abdominal pain or discomfort that occurs with altered bowel habits over a period of at least three months. Three subcategories of IBS have been identified: constipation-predominant (IBS-C), diarrhea-predominant (IBS-D), and mixed (IBS-M). British guidelines (2021) define IBS pragmatically as at least 6 months of abdominal pain or discomfort, in association with altered bowel habits, in the absence of alarm signs or symptoms.

list.listitem: Prevalence is approximately 10% to 15% of the US population, with a 2 to 1 female predominance.
In the United States, IBS accounts for up to 3.5 million physician visits annually.
IBS accounts for 20% to 50% of referrals to gastroenterology practices.
In the United States the median (interquartile range) annual IBS-specific spending was $1,127 (370-5,544) per patient with the highest spending observed in IBS with constipation at $2,222.
The etiology of IBS remains unclear.
Some IBS patients have been found to have microscopic inflammation, had a prior episode of acute diarrheal illness, have anxiety and depression, or have a history of physical/sexual abuse.
IBS has been recognized as a key component of the Gulf War Syndrome.
Antibiotic treatment is associated with an increased risk of IBS. More courses of antibiotics is associated with a higher rate of IBS diagnosis.
No structural or biochemical mechanism has been identified.
Physiologic components of the syndrome include disturbances in gastrointestinal motility, visceral afferent hypersenitivity, and central nervous system perception.
Rome IV criteria can be used to establish the diagnosis.C
Colonoscopy needs to be done only when alarm features are present.B
Use serologic testing to exclude celiac disease in patients with IBS with diarrhea, and fecal calprotectin to rule out inflammatory bowel disease.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Other endocrine symptoms (ie, weight change, temperature intolerance, alopecia, irregular menstruation)
Chronic severe diarrhea, anemia, weight loss, hematochezia
Anemia, weight loss, hematochezia, family history

list.listitem: The most recent diagnostic criteria is the Rome IV criteria (updated in 2016). It includes recurrent abdominal pain at least one day per week over three months with two or more of the following: related to defecation, associated with a change in stool frequency, and/or associated with a change in stool form (appearance).

Hallmark symptoms of IBS defined by the Manning criteria are abdominal pain relieved by defecation, abdominal pain associated with looser or more frequent stools, abdominal distension, the passage of mucus, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation after defecation.Patients also may experience constipation, alternating diarrhea and constipation, bloating or flatulance.
Symptoms are typically worse at times of increased stress and anxiety. Up to two-thirds will have a concomitant psychiatric disorder, most commonly anxiety or depression.
Physical examination is essentially normal without significant abdominal tenderness or distention. Guaiac examination of the stool should be negative.
Bristol stool types help define the subcategory of IBS, focusing most on types 1, 2, 6 and 7.

When patients present with “alarm” features, which include hematochezia, anemia, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, dysphagia, age over 50 years, and a family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or celiac sprue, further testing should be done to rule out other disease processes, generally with colonoscopy.

ACG guidelines recommend ordering endomysial or antitissue transglutaminase antibody in patients with IBS-D, IBS-M, and where celiac disease is suspected. A population based study of adults with abdominal symptoms found that 1% to 2% are diagnosed with celiac disease.
ACG guidelines also recommend ordering fecal calprotectin to rule-out inflammatory bowel disease.

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2021) recommend that initial evaluation in primary care should include a complete blood count, C-reactive protein or sedimentation rate, and serology for celiac disease. For patients younger than 45 years who present with diarrhea, order a fecal calprotectin test to rule out inflammatory bowel disease. Consider testing for bile acid diarrhea in patients with nocturnal diarrhea or prior cholecystectomy. The guidelines recommend against testing for pancreatic insufficiency, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, or carbohydrate intolerance if the symptoms are typical for IBS.

British guidelines (2021) recommend screening for colorectal cancer in accordance with national guidelines; colonoscopy is only recommended for patients with alarm signs and symptoms or who are at increased risk for microscopic colitis (female, at least 50 years old, with comorbid autoimmune disease; weight loss; diarrhea for less than 12 months; or severe, nocturnal, or watery diarrhea).
In one study, a normal calprotectin, a normal permeability ratio, and positive Rome criteria were highly accurate in ruling-in IBS.
ESR and CRP should not be elevated in IBS and, if elevated, should lead you to suspect an alternative diagnosis, such as Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
A focused history and physical examination, including rectal examination, is appropriate in all cases.
Rome IV criteria can be used to establish the diagnosis.

Order serology to exclude celiac disease, and fecal calprotectin to rule out inflammatory bowel disease. Consider CBC, CRP, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), electrolyte levels, and stool studies, including fecal occult blood testing in selected patients.
Celiac disese is highly prevalent in patients with IBS.
Patients older than 50 years and those with "alarm" features for malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease should be evaluated with colonoscopy.
Five psychological factors (physical fatigue, GI-specific anxiety, perceived stress, pain catastrophizing, and trait anxiety) demonstrated significant associations with GI symptom severity.
Exercise and increasing doses of soluble fiber (eg, ispaghula) but not insoluble fiber (eg, wheat bran) are recommended first-line treatments.B
Consider loperamide for diarrheal symptoms; antispasmodics and peppermint oil for global symptoms, as well as abdominal pain and cramping; and polyethylene glycol for constipation.B
Second-line drugs in primary care include tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.B
Behavioral therapies (in-person, digital, or delivered at a distance) may improve IBS symptoms.B
Tegaserod may be helpful in patients with IBS-C, and alosetron may be helpful in patients with IBS-D. However, these medications are only available for a select population or for severe cases.A
ACG guidelines recommend linaclotide, lubiprostone, or plecanatide for IBS-C.A They also recommend a trial of a low FODMAPS diet and gut-directed psychotherapy.B

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2021) recommend as first-line treatment gradually increasing doses of soluble fiber (eg, ispaghula) but not insoluble fiber (eg, wheat bran). They recommend considering probiotics, although the guideline doesn't recommend a specific species or dose. Consider loperamide for diarrheal symptoms; antispasmodics and peppermint oil for global symptoms, as well as abdominal pain and cramping; and polyethylene glycol for constipation.

The British guidelines recommend as second-line drugs in primary care tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Other drug classes, such as medications targeting 5-HT-3 and 5-HT-4 receptors, should be prescribed after evaluation by a gastroenterologist.

Antispasmodic agents, such as dicyclomine (Bentyl) and hyoscyamine (Levsin), can be used in all forms of IBS. In a systematic review, 7 of 11 studies were positive for relief of abdominal pain. The NNT was 7 for improvement in abdominal pain, 5 for improvement in global assessment, and 3 for improvement in symptom score. Some patients experience dry mouth, dizziness, and blurred vision (NNH = 18).

Low-dose antidepressants can be used when pain is the predominant symptom. TCAs may slow intestinal transit time and aid in the treatment of diarrhea (eg, amitriptyline). A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found evidence of symptom improvement (NNT = 3.2) over the short term.Another meta-analysis found antidepressants are beneficial (NNT = 4). SSRI can also be used when pain is present along with constipation.
Good evidence supports the use of antidepressants (TCAs and SSRIs) in IBS (NNT = 5). TCAs may be the most effective.

Amitriptyline is an effective second-line agent. A study randomized 463 persons with IBS who had persistent symptoms after first-line therapies. They were randomized to amitriptyline 10 mg titrated to 30 mg or placebo fo 6 months. Amitriptyline reduced symptom severity and the likelihood of relief of symptom (NNT=7 for meaningful improvement).

The 5-HT4 receptor agonist tegaserod (Zelnorm) is approved for use in women under 65 years of age with IBS-C without any known ischemic cardiovascular disease or no more than one CVD risk factor. A Cochrane review found modest improvement in overall symptoms and frequency of bowel movements for those with chronic constipation. Tegaserod was originally approved in 2002 but pulled from market in 2007 because of increased risk of serious cardiovascular events. It was re-released in 2019 with a more limited indication for usage.
A chloride channel activator, lubiprostone, is FDA approved for women over 18 years of age and is effective in constipation-predominant IBS compared to placebo.

Linaclotide (Linzess) 290 mcg once daily is approved for IBS-C and significantly improved multiple abdominal symptoms compared with placebo after 12 weeks. There are studies ongoing to see if a delayed-release formulation may help target just abdominal pain.

Tenapanor is a novel medicine that is a sodium/hyrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor that is currently approved in Canada for treatment of IBS-C. It showed symptom improved over 26 weeks with diarrhea being the predominant adverse effect. An ad-hoc analysis showed it significantly improved pain, discomfort, and bloating compared with placebo.
Minesapride is no more effective than placebo in constipation predominant IBS.
Plecanatide treatment improved IBS-C abdominal and bowel symptoms, including in those who present with moderate-to-severe bloating.

5-HT3 receptor antagonists can be used when diarrhea and/or pain in women is the predominant symptom. Their mechanism of action is through noxious stimuli perception, increasing colonic compliance, and decreasing gastrocolonic reflexes. Ondansetron has modest benefit in diarrhea-predominant IBS. Alosetron (Lotronex) has strict prescribing regulations and is reserved for patients who have failed conventional treatment. The NNT was 7 for improvement of symptoms.
Antidiarrheal agents such as loperamide (Imodium) can be used when diarrhea is the predominant symptom. They improve stool consistency and improve stool frequency.

Eluxadoline is a mu opioid receptor agonist that reduces symptoms in diarrhea-predominant IBS, with an NNT of 14 (75 mg BID) and 9 (100 mg BID) to reduce sypmtoms by 30% or more on 50% or more days. It is expensive and associated with rare but serious side effects.

Rifaximin may provide modest benefit in some patients with nonconstipation predominant IBS (NNT = 11). Treatment with 400 mg three times daily for 10 to 14 days appears to improve symptoms for 10 to 12 weeks.
Neomycin improved symptoms in one study, but symptoms recurred as soon as 2 weeks after treatment.

Peppermint oil (2 enteric-coated capsules twice daily) is thought to possess antispasmodic properties. Peppermint oil may be beneficial to reduce symptoms (NNT=4) but is associated with GI side effects (NNH = 7).
Several Chinese herbs have improved global symptoms in patients with IBS, but the quality of trials is generally low.

Probiotics have some benefit for improving IBS symptoms (NNT = 12). Some probiotic combinations may be effective. The effect is small to moderate.Preliminary evidence also suggests probiotics might be beneficial in children with IBS. Studies suggest that only specific bacterial strains of probiotics are beneficial in IBS.
Data are inconclusive with respect to acupuncture.
Hypnotherapy may be effective in kids with functional abdominal pain or IBS but data quality is poor.
Further study is needed with high-quality randomized trials before yoga can be recommended for IBS.
Acupuncture is effective for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea compared to sham acupuncture with an NNT of 6 to improve pain by 30% and diarrhea by 50% at six weeks.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), hypnotherapy, and stress management or relaxation therapy can be used as adjuncts to conventional treatment. CBT studies show mixed results. One RCT shows NNT = 6 to achieve moderate to substantial improvement in symptoms.
Behavioral therapy in one small study was effective as an add-on to medical treatment.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, hypotherapy, and pyschotherapy are all helpful for IBS patients. A systematic review concluded that CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy were most likely to be effective.

A systematic review of 42 RCTs with 5220 participants concluded that self-guided or minimal contact cognitive behavioral therapy, in person behavioral therapy, and in person gut-directed hypnotherapy appear to be effective.

A trial randomized adults with IBS to 42 daily sessions of a digital program for gut-directed hypnotherapy or usual care. Achieving a 50 point decrease in the IBS Symptom Severity Scale occurred more often with the intervention (81% vs 63%, p = .002, NNT = 5).

A diet low in fermentable, oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPS) can significantly decrease bloating, abdominal pain, and flatulence and a low-FODMAP-gluten free diet significantly enhances clinical symptoms and reduces anxiety and depression.
Increasing fluid and fiber intake in IBS-C can help relieve constipation.

Fiber, particularly soluble fiber, can be useful with all forms of IBS (ie, psyllium and guar gum) (NNT = 8). In an RCT of high-fiber supplements compared to guar gum, both improved symptoms equally but patients preferred guar gum.However, in a Cochrane review, bulking agents were not found to be effective for pain nor improved symptoms, although they may decrease constipation.

A randomized trial compared a low FODMAPS diet guided by an app with an antispasmodic drug (otilonium bromide) and found better results with the dietary intervention (77% vs 62% responders, p = 0.004, NNT = 7).
The Mediterranean diet is superior to traditional dietary advice with improved symptoms (NNT=5 at 6 weeks) and may be a viable first-line treatment option.
Exercise may improve symptoms in some patients. British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2021) recommend exercise as first-line treatment.

Data remains mixed on benefit of fecal microbiota transplant. Quality of donor stool may be an important factor. American Gastroenterology Association guidelines (2024) recommend against using fecal microbiota transplant outside the context of clinical trials.

Enterosgel (polymethylsiloxane polyhydrate) is an intestinal absorbent available over the counter (about $200/month supply). It was somewhat more effective than placebo in a randomized trial with more reporting adequate symptom relief at 8 weeks (69% vs 45%).
A small preliminary study showed transcutaneous auricular vagal stimulation may improve pain and constipation in adults with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation compared with sham therapy.
IBS is a common problem with considerable fluctuation of symptoms over time.B
Spontaneous resolution is common.B
A recent study in the UK found that having an IBS diagnosis was strongly associated with a decrease in all-cause (HR = 0.7) and all-cancer (HR = 0.69) related mortality over 10 years.
Children with IBS are likely to show spontaneous symptom resolution at 24 months.
In a small study (n = 53) of children recruited from a pediatric gastroenterology clinic, hypnotherapy was effective for children with functional abdominal pain or IBS.
A 13 week study found that amitriptyline appeared to improve quality of life somewhat in adolescents with IBS.

A randomized trial comparing placebo to a symptom diary and rescue analgesics found somewhat lower symptom scores while taking placebo. Notably, 3% of the children took rescue analgesics during the control period compared with 6.7% during the placebo period. That translates to a number needed to treat of 3 (95% CI 2 - 5).
